# 1. Working directories

The working directory is the default location where R will look for
files you want to load and where it will put any files you save.

You can also use the `getwd()` function in the Console which returns the
file path of the current working directory.

```{r}
getwd()


```

If you wanna set a directory

```{r}
setwd('/home/fer/Escritorio/U/Magister/Topicos Avanzados en Ciencias de Datos/Clase_Import_Data/Clase_Import_Data')
```

```{r}
getwd()
```

If you wanna list the files located into the directory

```{r}
list.files()
```

# 2. Importing data in R

Loading data into R can be quite frustrating. Almost every single type
of file that you want to get into R seems to require its function, and
even then, you might get lost in the functions' arguments. In short, it
can be fairly easy to mix up things from time to time, whether you are a
beginner or a more advanced R user.

## 2.1. Importing data to R from a CSV files

### 2.1.1 readr() function

In this section, we will read data in r by loading a CSV file from Hotel
Booking Demand. This dataset consists of booking data from a city hotel
and a resort hotel. To import the CSV file, we will use the readr
package's `read_csv` function.

readr supports the following file formats with these read\_\*()
functions:

read_csv(): comma-separated values (CSV)

read_tsv(): tab-separated values (TSV)

read_csv2(): semicolon-separated values with , as the decimal mark

read_delim(): delimited files (CSV and TSV are important special cases)

read_fwf(): fixed-width files

read_table(): whitespace-separated files

read_log(): web log files

```{r}
#library(readr)
# no es necesario hacerlo varias veces, en una sesion una pura vez basta
data1 <- read_csv('hotel_bookings_clean.csv', show_col_types = FALSE)

head(data1)
```

```{r}
?read_csv()
```

`read_csv()` and `read_tsv()` are special cases of the more general
`read_delim()`. They're useful for reading the most common types of flat
file data, comma separated values and tab separated values,
respectively. `read_csv2()` uses ⁠;⁠ for the field separator and ⁠,⁠ for the
decimal point.

```{r}
library(readr)

data_tab <- read_delim('hotel_bookings_clean.csv', delim = ',', show_col_types = FALSE)

data_tab
```

### 2.1.2. read.table() function

Similar to `read_csv` you can also use the `read.table` function to load
the file. Make sure you are adding delimiter "," and header = 1. It will
set the first row as column names instead of "V1", "V2",...

```{r}
data2 <- read.table('hotel_bookings_clean.csv', sep=",", header = 1)


head(data2, 5)
```

### 2.1.3. Comparing the timing of these functions

```{r}
timing_result <- system.time({
    data1 <- read_csv('hotel_bookings_clean.csv', show_col_types = FALSE)
})

# Print the result and timing information
print(timing_result)
```

```{r}
timing_result <- system.time({
    data_tab <- read_delim('hotel_bookings_clean.csv', delim = ',', show_col_types = FALSE)
})

# Print the result and timing information
print(timing_result)
```

```{r}
timing_result <- system.time({
    data2 <- read.table('hotel_bookings_clean.csv', sep=",", header = 1)
})

# Print the result and timing information
print(timing_result)
```

## 2.2. Importing a TXT file in R

In this part, we will use the Canserbero Lyrics dataset to load a text
file. The file consists of Lyrics from the rapper Canserbero. We can use
the `readLines` function to load the simple file, but we have to perform
additional tasks to convert it into a dataframe.

We will use read.table's alternative function, `read.delim` to load the
text file as an R dataframe. Other read.table's alternative functions
are read.csv, read.csv2, and read.delim2.

```{r}
data3 <- read.delim('Canserbero_lyrics.txt', header = F)
head(data3, 5)
```

## 2.3. Importing data from Excel into R

We will use the readxl package's `read_excel` function to read a single
sheet from an Excel file. The package comes with tiddyvers, but it is
not the core part of it, so we need to load the package before using the
function.

The function requires the location of the data and sheet number. We can
also modify how our dataframe looks by reading the description of other
parameters in read_excel documentation.

```{r}
library(readxl)
data4 <- read_excel("hotel_bookings_clean.xlsx", sheet = "Sheet1", col_names = TRUE)

head(data4, 5)
```

```{r}
?read_excel()
```

## 2.4. Importing some columns from excel

```{r}
library(readxl)
data4 <- read_excel("hotel_bookings_clean.xlsx", sheet = "Sheet1", col_names = TRUE, range = cell_cols("A:D"))

head(data4, 5)

```

```{r}
library(openxlsx)

data4 <- read.xlsx("hotel_bookings_clean.xlsx", cols = 10:20)

head(data4)
```

```{r}
library(readxl)
data4 <- read_excel("hotel_bookings_clean.xlsx", sheet = "Sheet1", col_names = TRUE)[1:7]


head(data4)
```

## 2.5. Importing some rows from excel

```{r}
library(readxl)

data4 <- read_excel("hotel_bookings_clean.xlsx", sheet = "Sheet1", col_names = TRUE)

dim(data4)

data_slice <- data4[1:40, ]

dim(data_slice)
head(data_slice)
```
